title: Distributed Unique ID Generator
intro: Generate globally unique 64-bit roughly time-ordered IDs at 100,000+ QPS without central database auto-increment bottlenecks.
objectives: Deconstruct Twitter Snowflake 64-bit layout (timestamp, datacenter, worker, sequence).
Mitigate NTP backward clock drift in production servers.
Compare UUIDv4 vs Snowflake for relational database B-tree index locality.
body:
### The Twitter Snowflake Layout
A 64-bit integer fitting standard SQL `BIGINT` primary keys:
- **1 sign bit**: Always 0 (positive integer).
- **41-bit Timestamp**: Milliseconds elapsed since a custom epoch (e.g. Nov 2024). $2^{41}$ ms $\approx 69$ years of lifespan.
- **5-bit Datacenter ID**: Supports up to 32 datacenters.
- **5-bit Worker ID**: Supports up to 32 worker machines per datacenter (1,024 total nodes).
- **12-bit Sequence Counter**: Increments for IDs generated within the exact same millisecond ($2^{12} = 4,096$ IDs/ms per worker $\approx 4.09$ million IDs/sec per machine).
keyIdea: Roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs preserve database B-tree index insertion locality and eliminate locking across distributed nodes.

concepts.title: B-Tree Locality vs UUIDv4
concepts.body: Random 128-bit UUIDv4 scatters inserts across random B-tree pages, triggering massive disk I/O page thrashing. Snowflake IDs insert sequentially at the end of the B-tree leaf pages.

concepts.title: Clock Skew Mitigation
concepts.body: If NTP jumps system time backward, the generator detects `current_time < last_timestamp` and pauses until the clock catches up, or throws a hardware clock alert.

examples: Discord utilizing Snowflake IDs for all messages and channels.

quiz.prompt: Why does UUIDv4 degrade database insertion throughput compared to Snowflake IDs?
options: UUIDs are stored as encrypted blobs
Randomness in UUIDv4 causes B-Tree page splits and random disk I/O thrashing
UUIDs cannot be indexed in SQL
UUID generation requires synchronous network RPCs
quiz.explanation: UUIDv4 random values force writes into arbitrary pages throughout the B-tree, causing frequent page splits and cache misses.
